vignette:
Marisol, a 39-year-old married woman who worked in nonprofit outreach, described the assault as the event that split her life into “before and after,” though even that phrase felt too simple to her because the memory itself never came back in a clean line. She had been leaving a community meeting after dusk, carrying a tote bag and a folder of intake paperwork, when a man approached with a weapon in his hand and the night suddenly narrowed to fear, confusion, and the unbearable awareness of her own vulnerability. She remembered fragments rather than a sequence: the shine of metal, the sense that her body had gone cold, the sound of her own breathing, the violent fact of being overpowered. When she tried to tell people what happened, she could say only pieces. She knew what happened, but she could not find words that held it together, and the missing order of it disturbed her almost as much as the assault itself. Months later, when she tried to speak about it, the story still came out in stops and starts, as if the memory resisted being placed in time.

In the days and weeks that followed, Marisol noticed that certain sights and situations hit her with immediate force. Anything that looked like a weapon, or even an object that could be used as one, made her body tighten before she had time to think. A box cutter on a worktable, a metal rod leaning against a wall, a stranger’s hand gripping a heavy flashlight in the parking lot after an evening meeting could make her stomach drop. She also became acutely distressed by any reminder of nakedness or exposure. The memory of being physically overpowered had left her feeling stripped of control, and even ordinary moments such as changing clothes in a locker room or stepping out of the shower could bring back a flash of the fear she had felt at the assault. She did not describe these reactions as dramatic; she spoke of them as immediate and private, the body recognizing danger faster than the mind could argue with it.

By the time she sought help, Marisol was living with persistent jumpiness. A door closing too hard, footsteps behind her, a voice raised unexpectedly in a hallway at work could send a jolt through her so fast that she would flinch before realizing she was reacting. She found it impossible to believe other people when they told her she was safe. Even in familiar places, reassurance slid off her; if someone said the building was secure or that the neighborhood was fine, she could hear the words but could not make them feel true. Night was hardest. During the day she could usually stay busy enough to manage, but after dark she became watchful in a way that exhausted her. At home she checked locks repeatedly and preferred to keep lights on in rooms she passed through. If her husband went out, she watched the clock and listened for sounds outside, convinced that darkness made the world more open to harm. She would lie awake alert to every noise, feeling that night itself carried a different kind of threat.

Her work had also become the place where reminders appeared most concretely. As a nonprofit worker, Marisol spent her days in offices, neighborhood centers, and community spaces where she once felt connected and useful. After the assault, that connection changed. She found herself less able to feel part of the community and culture that had always given meaning to her work. Meetings that used to feel energizing now reminded her of what she had lost, and she was saddened by how separate she felt from the people she served and from the cultural familiarity that had once grounded her. She spoke with grief about feeling cut off, as though the assault had not only happened to her body but had also taken her out of a shared world she no longer fully inhabited.

Marisol’s thoughts about herself had become harsh and persistent. She called herself weak, saying there must have been something in her that made her vulnerable in the first place. She compared herself to other people and was certain someone else would not have ended up in that situation. Even though she knew, intellectually, that the assault was the responsibility of the person who attacked her, she kept returning to the belief that she should have done something different, moved faster, seen more, prevented it somehow. When she remembered the event, a hot wave of rage rose in her, directed at the assailant, at the injustice of what happened, and at the helplessness she still felt when the memory surfaced.

She finally came for help after realizing how much her life had narrowed. She was tired of living in a state of constant alert, tired of checking shadows at night, tired of shrinking from objects that looked dangerous and of feeling disconnected from the community work that had once been central to her identity. What frightened her most was the sense that the world could still become unsafe without warning and that she might never fully trust it again. What she hoped for, though she said it cautiously, was to be able to walk into her own home at night, go through her workday, and remember the assault without being overwhelmed by fragments, rage, or the feeling that she had been changed into someone smaller than she used to be.
